SCHOOL CHILDREN WITH NO SCHOOL

By: Ntokozo Miya | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Last year, Gauteng's education department assured parents that every child would be placed at a school but 162 learners have not been inside a classroom this year – what went wrong?

Unique Selling Point:
We confront the education department about how it came about that 162 children were left without a school and are still not placed nine months into the year.

Summary:
In November 2019, parents expressed concerns about late placements and not getting the schools of their choice for their children. The department assured parents, and Carte Blanche during an interview, that EVERY child would be placed at a school and would have access to learning.
Even with the lockdown messing up the school calendar, children who were placed in schools were able to learn online through their respective school programs.
But it's now the end of September and 162 children in Gauteng have yet to be placed. Because these children were not officially registered to any school, they were unable to participate in online learning programs and had to keep themselves busy with whatever material their parents found for them.

Further information:
At the beginning of the year, the department made provision for these learners to be accommodated in the halls of nearby schools. For about three weeks, the children, in grade 8 to 10, had a rotation of teachers who came to the halls. That did not last as it was difficult to coordinate and manage learning time between their own classes and the addittional students. The children were then left to fend for themselves, literally just passing the time idling at these school halls.
When the lockdown came, schools were closed but some learners were able to continue classes online. This was not the case for the 162 children who do not officially belong to any school.
When schools reopened, the schools that had housed the unplaced children declined to accept these kids into the halls, citing concerns about social distancing and possible exposure to and spread of the coronavirus.
With all the learners now back in school, these children remain at home. Parents demand answers

SCHOOLCHILDREN WITH NO SCHOOL



INTRO – The relaxation of lockdown restrictions has brought with it some semblance of normality – most learners are now back in class to salvage what's left of the academic year.
However, the national education department is concerned that between ten and twenty per cent of learners across the country have not yet returned to school.
But some Gauteng parents say the lockdown has had no impact on their children because even before the lockdown, these children hadn't set foot inside a classroom.
LINK – The South African schools act stipulates that every child between the age of seven and fifteen must attend school, but what happens when a child hasn't been allocated a school to attend?
VO – Last year, the Gauteng education department had to calm angry parents after its online placement system allocated them schools that were far from their homes.
At the time, department spokesperson Steve Mabona said there would be placement delays due to limited capacity, but every child would get a spot in class even if it wasn't at the school of their choice.
UPSOUND – STEVE MABONA – GAUTENG DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION – CARTE BLANCHE - NOVEMBER 2019
We'll never get tired to apologise to all our parents. We are just hoping that they will understand that capacity is our challenge.
VO – Thousands of learners were indeed placed, but one hundred and sixty-two children in the south of Johannesburg were only registered with the department but were not actually placed at a school that they would attend.
Applications for 2021 have already begun but parents are concerned that if the department could not accommodate these learners, it may not be prepared for the influx of next year's learners.
VO - Lebohang Khola applied for her son Thato to do grade 8 but the youngster's excitement at starting high school this year was quickly snuffed out.
LEBOHANG KHOLA – PARENT
They told us that there is no school. There is no space for our kids.
VO – The department had a plan.
LEBOHANG KHOLA – PARENT
They were placed there at a school hall. They told us that it was a temporary situation.
VO – Five teachers took turns giving classes to the unplaced learners but that only lasted for three weeks.
THATO KHOLA – UNPLACED LEARNER
One teacher is teaching 150 of us so if you're sitting maybe at the back, you can't hear.
VO – When schools closed for the lockdown, learners who were allocated a school continued with the curriculum online. Thato could only rely on whatever study material his mother could get.
THATO KHOLA – UNPLACED LEARNER
It's not going to help me because I need to get it from a teacher.
VO – When classes resumed recently, social distancing protocols meant that the host school could not house additional learners.
The placement ordeal is especially heartbreaking for Lebohang because ironically, she is a teacher.
LEBOHANG KHOLA – PARENT
I wake up everyday to go and teach other learners, other children but mine is still at home.
VO – Two weeks ago, one hundred and sixty-two learners were stranded. Since then, the department says it has placed twenty-four.
Failure to place children at school is a violation of learners' rights, explains Tarryn Cooper-Bell, supervising attorney at the Equal Education Law Centre.
TARRYN COOPER-BELL – EQUAL EDUCATION LAW CENTRE – UPSOUND
It may therefore be appropriate to now start approaching the courts to seek relief, appropriate relief in this situation.
VO – Professor Mary Metcalfe has worked in the education sector for nearly five decades. She says school capacity problems are brought on by the massive movement of people closer to areas of opportunities.
PROF. MARY METCALFE – EDUCATION EXPERT – interviews project
We see it in the north of Johannesburg where there has been extensive building development that's commercially driven without schools being provided. And we see it in the south in this particular affected area.
VO – She suggests that parents engage the department about solutions.
But Mandla Xaba says it's difficult to negotiate with authorities because they never keep their promises. Mandla's son applied for grade 9 this year.
MANDLA XABA – PARENT
This is the space that the department of education actually put aside to say that this is where they are going to build the school for all the kids that were not accommodated. We are supposed to already be having the classes, the movable classes for the kids.The space is still empty.
VO – Another parent, Christina Ferreira, says it's disappointing that the department’s spokesperson Steve Mabona ignores their urgent concerns but has been vocal in the media.
CHRISTINA FERREIRA – PARENT
We even say he's lying because he'll be saying: “All the kids are placed.” And we'd be like: “WHAT?!” I have a child sitting at home and you're telling me all the kids are placed.
VO - Her son, who applied to be in grade 8 this year is not coping well with the situation.
CHRISTINA FERREIRA – PARENT
He even asked me: “Mommy, why not private school?” I went to private school and the fees, I cannot afford.
LINK – The parents we spoke to say that their children are the victims of the online placement system, that the education department continues to stand by.
VO – Mabona says the challenge is not the system but rather, increasing schools' capacity to accommodate more learners.
STEVE MABONA – GAUTENG EDUCATION DEPARTMENT
CLAIRE – Will it not only get more difficult and a bigger problem going forward in terms of capacity?
MABONA – Look, we acknowledge that we have a challenge in the Johannesburg south. The process of identifying schools that are capable of expanding, we have not stopped with that.
VO – He says the department has not lied to parents or the media – the children may not be in a classroom but they are registered learners with the department and should be getting learning material from the host school.
STEVE MABONA – GAUTENG EDUCATION DEPARTMENT
We will make sure that our officials verify that is there any learner that did not receive material so that we finalise that process but the school that is supporting them did not say we can support only a certain number, they gave us an assurance that we're supporting all of them.
VO – The department plans to meet with parents to discuss school placement, and ways to assist learners to prepare for final assessments, even at this late stage.
STEVE MABONA – GAUTENG EDUCATION DEPARTMENT
It's unfortunate but that can be rectified because of this meeting that they will be facilitating over the weekend.
VO – The department says these learners will not go through the online placement process and will be prioritised for 2021.
But unless the unplaced learners are able to get through months of schoolwork and complete the necessary assessments in record time, they cannot be promoted to higher grades next year.
TARRYN COOPER-BELL – EQUAL EDUCATION LAW CENTRE – UPSOUND
And that is a severe failure by the education department, the fact that a learner has now wasted a year of basically not being able to be educated.
VO – Thato has not yet come to terms with the possibility of doing grade eight next year. If the department keeps its promise to provide learning and assessment support, he says he is prepared to work hard to earn his promotion.
THATO KHOLA – UNPLACED LEARNER
CLAIRE – Will you be able to cope because we haven't learned much this year?
THATO – I think I will.


PROMOS

One hundred and sixty-two children have not been inside a classroom this year. If the
Gauteng education department couldn't accommodate them, is it prepared for next year's
influx of learners?

We investigate why more than one hundred children have missed a year of school after
the Gauteng education department promised that it's online placement system would
place every learner.

More than one hundred children were not allocated schools to attend this year and
parents worry that next year, Gauteng's online placement system could leave even more
children out in the cold.
